Acq notes (acq): The vendor, F W Burt, acquired this collection from "a native of Apapa in 1907 who found them with some old pots while digging a water hole. Apapa is in the lagoon at Lagos, and is part of the mainland". T A Joyce (1930) reported that the group was 'excavated ten feet deep at Apapa near the lagoon' and was 'the most important find of bronzes yet discovered outside the Benin region.'

Description: Miniature bow made of iron, and iron wire.;
Curators Comments: Miniature metal bows and arrows of this kind are hunters' charms, the emblem of the Yoruba orisa Osoosi, the divinity in charge of hunting. See 'Arts du Nigeria', Paris 1997, cats.75 to 78, and Len Pole, ‘Iwa L’Ewa. Yoruba & Benin collections in the Royal Albert Museum, Exeter,’ 1999, cat.36. This example lacks the arrow seen in other examples.

Description: Register 1920: Velvet brown cap lined with silk; a gold foil inverted crescent is stitched on the front, and silver foil crocodiles on either side, an…
Curators Comments: This cap was donated to the British Museum together with the gown Af1920,0211.1 (qv). It presumably belongs with it and shares the same provenance. The cap itself is made of imported velvet; the cut-out foil appliqué of a crocodile is characteristic of Dahomey, and the cap was most probably made there.

Curators Comments: Read & Dalton 1899: Ivory spoon with deep shaped bowl, and "rat-tail" rib at the back. The handle is elaborately decorated in imitation of turning. Description: Wrapper; composed of two panels, hand sewn together. Each panel has varying width stripes in beige cotton, white, and different shades of indigo-dyed …
Curators Comments: Such a two-panel cloth is woven by women on an upright loom. This cloth and 2018,2036.277 were woven in a western Yoruba community living in the modern country of Benin (formerly Dahomey). Very little is know about weaving in that country, although there is abundant evidence that it was widely practised there, and very few examples have been collected or otherwise documented.

He died in 1900 at Kumasi during the fifth Anglo-Ashanti War.

Description: Salt currency. Block of salt broken into three pieces and tied together with a leaf.;
Curators Comments: Salt currency was one of the most accepted forms of exchange in Ethiopia. There are numerous records that illustrate that salt was often preferred than any other form of payment. Salt bars were used for barter, as small change, but they were also legal tender for taxes or fines.

Curators Comments: This painting follows a tradition of secular painting in Ethiopia which began in the late 19th/ early 20th century. The Emperor seated in judgement over his people, with the punishments inflicted on those who transgressed the law shown in graphic detail, became a popular theme. It can perhaps be seen as an allegory to the Biblical Day of Judgement.

Curators Comments: The forerunner of the vuvuzela is said to have been 'invented' in the 1960s by Freddie Maake who adapted it from a bicycle hooter. Maake created the name vuvuzela in 1992 to mark the release of Nelson Mandela. The name derives from three Zulu words meaning 'welcome', 'unite' and 'celebration'. Thousands of such horns were played by fans in South Africa for the 2010 World Cup.

Acq notes (acq): Af1919.1118.1 to 22 is a collection formed by the Rev.Neville Jones of the London Missionary Society, and sold by him to the BM. Curators Comments: Register: "Beer-strainer. Matabili."

Curators Comments: The working of glass into beads was very important in the Classical Period in Ife. At this time it seems likely that glass beads were imported across the Sahara from northern Europe or the Middle East and were then re-worked. The Olokun Grove appears to have been a centre of this glass-working industry although examples of beads and crucibles such as this one have been found in many Ife sites.

See Af1950,45.523, and H M Cole & C C Aniakor, 'Igbo arts, community and cosmos', UCLA 1984, pp.62-3. The finest (okwa oji) have a central cavity with a lid, in which condiments (such as pepper mashed with peanuts) are placed. They have been traditionally described in the BM as 'platters'.

Description: Fringed bag made of leather.;
Curators Comments: Af1934,0605.55 to 59 appear to belong together, and seem to derive from a single acquisition made in Kordofan of leather trappings for a camel. The bag (no.59) is recognisably of a Hausa type, made in northern Nigeria (Kano area) (cf Af1927,1207.44). On the assumption that they form a single group, it would seem likely that all were made in Nigeria and ended up on a camel in Kordofan.

Description: Camel trapping: bridle made of leather, with iron bit.;
Curators Comments: Af1934,0605.55 to 59 appear to belong together, and seem to derive from a single acquisition made in Kordofan of leather trappings for a camel. The bag (no.59) is recognisably of a Hausa type, made in northern Nigeria (Kano area). On the assumption that they form a single group, it would seem likely that all were made in Nigeria and ended up on a camel in Kordofan.

Curators Comments: Af1934,0605.55 to 59 appear to belong together, and seem to derive from a single acquisition made in Kordofan of leather trappings for a camel.
